item.title: Coupling Enzyme Activity to Host Survival via Genetic Code Expansion: An In Vivo Evolution System for Biocatalysts.
item.abstract: Survival-based selection facilitates the exploration of enzyme mutational space, but coupling the activity of noncanonical amino acid (ncAA)-producing biocatalysts to host survival remains challenging. Here, we report an in vivo selection platform that links biocatalyst activity to host cell survival via genetic code expansion. In this system, the intracellularly generated ncAA serves as a substrate for an orthogonal aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (aaRS). Its incorporation triggers the readthrough of an amber (TAG) stop codon to yield a functional chloramphenicol resistance protein, allowing cells harboring active biocatalyst variants to survive under antibiotic selection. The applicability of this approach was validated using three biocatalysts: tyrosine phenol-lyase (TPL), tryptophan synthase β-subunit (TrpB), and a hydrolytic carbamoylase (SmLcar). Using this directed evolution system, we evolved TPL and TrpB to process previously inactive substrates, enabling the gram-scale preparative biosynthesis of target ncAAs with final titers reaching 36.8 g/L. Furthermore, because cell survival requires both in vivo ncAA synthesis and its subsequent orthogonal translation, this dual dependency enables the simultaneous selection of upstream biocatalysts and downstream aaRS variants. Leveraging this mechanism, we performed the selection of TPL and chPylRS libraries simultaneously, yielding enzyme pairs for the generation and recognition of target ncAAs. This platform provides a powerful tool for the directed evolution of ncAA-producing biocatalysts.

item.title: Upgrading yeast-based low-carbon biomanufacturing by harnessing a universal in vivo evolution system.
item.abstract: Non-conventional yeasts are emerging as key cell factories in low-carbon biomanufacturing, but unlocking their full potential requires optimizing complex traits, such as substrate utilization and high-level protein expression, through in vivo genome-wide evolution. To address this, we developed a universal plasmid vector deploying a DNA Helicase-Activation-Induced Cytidine Deaminase (Helicase-AID) for genome-wide base editing. This system enables cross-species mutagenesis in diverse yeasts, including Yarrowia lipolytica, Pichia pastoris, and Kluyveromyces marxianus. We demonstrated that MCM5-AID base editing efficiency in Y. lipolytica is time-dependent, achieving a cumulative mutation rate of 3.13 × 10-5 mutations per base pair (bp-1) over 432 hours. Using this system, we evolved Y. lipolytica variants exhibiting a 37.77% increase in maximum specific growth rate on acetate, alongside altered starch production ranging from -92.96% to 17.45%. Crucially, we utilized this platform to activate the silent expression of heterologous proteins, overcoming a persistent bottleneck in microbial strain engineering. Evolutionary, transcriptomic and genomic analyses showed that evolved Y. lipolytica variants exhibited enhanced accumulation of Cas13x, a naturally difficult-to-express protein, via reduced proteolytic degradation. In contrast, evolved P. pastoris variants gained the ability to express previously silent thaumatin through significant transcriptional upregulation, enhanced protein folding, and increased amino acid biosynthesis. Ultimately, this universal in vivo evolution system provides a robust platform for genome-directed evolution across diverse industrial yeast species, accelerating the systematic exploration of their potential in low-carbon biomanufacturing.

item.title: Programmable interphyla communication for Staphylococcus aureus by transferability of homoserine lactone sensors between Bacillales bacteria
item.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive opportunistic pathogen of the order Bacillales and a frequent member of human-associated microbiomes. Despite its clinical relevance, engineering S. aureus and the communities it inhabits remains limited by a shortage of well-characterized genetic tools for precise control of gene expression and intercellular signaling. Biosensors for homoserine lactones (HSLs) are widely used in Gram-negative bacteria, as HSLs are small, passively diffusible signaling molecules for and their sensors are tightly regulated. Here, we show that synthetically designed HSL sensors using LuxR-family regulators are highly functional in S. aureus. Notably, synthetic designs previously built for the Gram-positive model Bacillus subtilis, a distantly related Bacillales, transferred functionally and establish repurposing the genetic toolbox as an effective strategy for importing these functions into S. aureus. Sensor performance correlated strongly between the two Bacillales, and activation in S. aureus reached 55-fold, exceeding the dynamic range of reported inducible systems. We further demonstrate tightly regulated, programmable interphyla communication between Gram-negative Escherichia coli and S. aureus via HSL signaling. These results provide a new toolset for engineering interbacterial communication and open a route to extending programmable HSL signaling to other tough-to-engineer bacteria.

item.title: Engineered bacteriophages as precision antimicrobials against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: molecular engineering strategies, clinical translation, and the crystallizing global regulatory landscape.
item.abstract: The global antimicrobial resistance crisis, driven primarily by the ESKAPE pathogen consortium has catalyzed the translation of engineered bacteriophage therapeutics from experimental platforms to clinical-stage precision medicines. Unlike their wild-type counterparts, which are constrained by narrow host ranges, susceptibility to reticuloendothelial clearance, and limited biofilm penetrability, synthetically engineered phages exploit receptor-binding protein remodeling, phage-derived enzymatic depolymerases, CRISPR-Cas3 chromosomal shredding payloads, sequence-independent SASPject delivery vectors, and in vivo microbiome base editors to overcome the multilayered resistance arsenals of MDR ESKAPE organisms. Recent clinical development has generated human evidence across both genetically engineered phage platforms and advanced fixed phage-cocktails. Engineered programmes include CRISPR-Cas3-based LBP-EC01 and SNIPR001, while AP-SA02 represents an analytically characterized fixed multi-phage cocktail targeting Staphylococcus aureus. This review examines engineering strategies, pharmacokinetics, immune-mediated clearance, delivery challenges, clinical evidence, manufacturing, and regulatory pathways. It also discusses emerging regulatory approaches and distinctions between natural and genetically modified phage products. The literature search was conducted from January-June 2026 using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, supplemented by searches of ClinicalTrials.gov and the websites of the US-FDA and EMA. Overall, this review evaluates the translational potential of engineered phages, identifies barriers to clinical adoption, and considers future developments in precision antimicrobial therapy against multidrug-resistant pathogens.

item.title: Probing the biomolecular design space with generative modeling.
item.abstract: Discovering new-to-nature biomolecules requires navigating a design space that has only been sparsely explored. Traditional paradigms such as rational design, directed evolution, and high-throughput screening have enabled the development of many successful functional biomolecules, but are significantly limited when given an unseen target or novel function, where there is no starting point for design. Generative modeling offers a way to approximate the continuous manifold underlying observed biological data, enabling the sampling of new candidates beyond any finite dataset while remaining within the support of viable, functional biomolecules. Here, we outline recent progress in generative biomolecular design through an algorithmic lens, bridging theoretical foundations with its extensions and applications in truly de novo and controllable biomolecular design.

item.title: High-Throughput Dual-Optical Droplet Screening for Quantitative Functional Bacterial Selection.
item.abstract: Droplet microfluidics enables ultra-high-throughput biological screening, yet most platforms rely on single-parameter optical detection, limiting the information available for selection and analysis. Here, we present a high-throughput droplet screening and sorting platform that integrates simultaneous fluorescence and absorbance (scattering) detection with acoustic actuation for robust, kHz-rate operation. By combining complementary optical modalities within a single device, we enable multi-parameter characterization and sorting of droplets based on both molecular and cellular properties. We first validate the system using model droplets containing defined combinations of fluorophores and absorbers, achieving on-demand sorting of multiple sub-populations with efficiencies exceeding 97% at kilohertz rates. We then demonstrate biological functionality by quantifying bacterial growth via optical density (scattering/absorbance) and protein expression via green fluorescent protein (GFP) fluorescence within the same droplets. This dual readout enables simultaneous assessment of cell proliferation and gene expression and allows normalization of fluorescence signals to cell number, providing single-cell-level insight within droplets. Importantly, we observe a temporal delay of ∼42 min between growth and fluorescence signals, highlighting the dynamic relationship between cell proliferation and protein expression. The ability to resolve and exploit such multi-parameter dynamics enables more precise selection of functional phenotypes, including differentiation of sub-populations based on growth and expression characteristics. This integrated acoustofluidic platform provides a versatile and scalable approach for multi-parameter droplet analysis and sorting, with applications in microbiology, diagnostics, and directed evolution, where simultaneous measurement of the cellular state and function is critical.

item.title: CRISPR Technology: From Bench to Bedside Applications.
item.abstract: CRISPR-Cas genome editing represents one of the most transformative advances in modern molecular biology, enabling programmable site-specific genetic modification that has revolutionized functional genomics and precision therapeutic development. Beyond canonical Cas9 nucleases, the CRISPR toolkit has diversified into precision base editors, prime editors, CRISPR-associated transposases, and Cas12/Cas13 RNA-targeting effectors, each with distinct mechanistic properties. Clinically, ex vivo CRISPR therapies for hemoglobinopathies have secured regulatory approval, while base editing, prime editing, and in vivo Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T candidates are advancing through trials for a broad spectrum of hematologic, oncologic, and rare genetic disorders. However, existing reviews largely address technical innovation or clinical translation in isolation, lacking a holistic, up-to-date synthesis of the full bench-to-bedside trajectory of CRISPR technology. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms, advantages, and limitations of core CRISPR editing platforms; summarizes pivotal clinical data across hemoglobinopathies, CAR-T immunotherapy, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cardiometabolic diseases and rare monogenic diseases; evaluates delivery systems including lipid nanoparticles and viral vectors; and discusses key translational barriers such as off-target genotoxicity and immunogenicity alongside emerging optimization strategies. This work provides a holistic bench-to-bedside framework for CRISPR research, offering critical insights to advance next-generation precision genetic medicine.

item.title: SeekRBP: Leveraging Sequence-Structure Integration with Reinforcement Learning for Receptor-Binding Protein Identification.
item.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Receptor-binding proteins (RBPs) initiate viral infection and determine host specificity, serving as key targets for phage engineering and therapy. However, the identification of RBPs is complicated by their extreme sequence divergence, which often renders traditional homology-based alignment methods ineffective. While machine learning offers a promising alternative, such approaches struggle with severe class imbalance and the difficulty of selecting informative negative samples from heterogeneous tail proteins. Existing methods often fail to balance learning from these "hard negatives" while maintaining generalization.
RESULTS: We present SeekRBP, a sequence-structure framework that models negative sampling as a sequential decision-making problem. By employing a multi-armed bandit strategy, SeekRBP dynamically prioritizes informative non-RBP sequences based on real-time training feedback, complemented by a multimodal fusion of protein language and structural embeddings. Benchmarking demonstrates that SeekRBP consistently outperforms static sampling strategies. Furthermore, a case study on Vibrio phages validates that SeekRBP effectively identifies RBPs to improve host prediction, highlighting its potential for large-scale annotation and synthetic biology applications.
AVAILABILITY: The source code of SeekRBP is available via: https://github.com/Saillxl/SeekRBP.

item.title: Reprogramming flavonoid glycosylation by bridging advanced biocatalysis and systems synthetic biology.
item.abstract: Flavonoid glycosides exhibit profound pharmacological and nutritional value, yet their industrial-scale acquisition is severely hampered by low abundance in plant extracts and the stereochemical complexity of chemical synthesis. Synthetic biology offers a sustainable alternative, while the deployment of natural plant uridine diphosphate-dependent glycosyltransferases (UGTs) is intrinsically bottlenecked by low catalytic efficiency, poor stability, and severe intracellular metabolic competition. This review systematically explores the paradigm shifts in the biomanufacturing of these complex molecules, highlighting how the methodological evolution in UGT discovery has evolved from traditional sequence homology to multi-omics and AI-driven predictive models. Multidimensional engineering of UGTs spanning from active-site remodeling to distal allosteric regulation and computational-design is elucidated to precisely manipulate catalytic efficacy, enzyme stability, substrate promiscuity, and catalytic regioselectivity. Bridging the gap between optimized biocatalysts and robust microbial cell factories requires critical systems metabolic engineering strategies, including the rewiring of intracellular UDP-sugar flux, the elimination of catabolic sinks, and the deployment of spatiotemporally decoupled microbial consortia. Cell-free synthesis cascades offer a highly controllable alternative to circumvent in vivo physiological constraints. A strategic roadmap for future research emphasizes AI-driven de novo enzyme design, autonomous single-cell dynamic regulation, and the valorization of lignocellulosic biomass to achieve unprecedented atom economy. Ultimately, this integrated framework provides a scalable, multidimensional blueprint for the sustainable and green biomanufacturing of high-value flavonoid glycosides.

Despite their conserved catalytic architecture, type III PKSs exhibit remarkable plasticity in starter-substrate utilization, chain extension, and cyclization chemistry. This versatility makes them attractive but challenging targets for enzyme engineering. This review examines three major strategies for improving type III PKSs: screening and genome mining, structure-guided engineering, and directed evolution coupled with high-throughput screening or selection. We discuss how these approaches can be used to improve catalytic activity, substrate specificity, and product selectivity, both in vitro and in heterologous production hosts. We also examine recent applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to enzyme discovery, functional prediction, and variant prioritization, as well as the limitations imposed by small and heterogeneous datasets. Finally, we provide a practical framework for selecting engineering strategies and discuss future directions toward more predictable engineering of type III PKSs.

item.title: Stimuli-responsive CRISPR-based genome editing delivery system for cancer treatment: A review of fundamentals and applications.
item.abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Conventional modalities, namely surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, continue to face substantial limitations. The advent of gene therapy, particularly CRISPR-based genome editing, offers new opportunities to overcome these barriers. Nuclease systems such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable precise excision of mutant alleles and targeted insertion of exogenous sequences by harnessing endogenous DNA-repair pathways, achieving durable and accurate genomic modification; derivative tools including CRISPRi, base editing, and prime editing enable diverse forms of gene regulation or precise genome modification through transcriptional repression, base conversion, or related editing mechanisms. To enhance the efficiency, specificity, and spatiotemporal control of CRISPR editing in vivo, sophisticated delivery platforms have been engineered to respond to endogenous tumor-microenvironment cues (e.g., pH, redox potential, hypoxia, ATP, enzymes and microRNAs) or exogenous triggers (e.g., light, ultrasound and magnetic fields). Distinct from material-centric classification schemes, this review organizes these stimuli-responsive systems according to their pathological relevance to the tumor microenvironment (TME), establishing a conceptual framework that links specific TME aberrations with corresponding delivery paradigms. These stimuli-responsive systems represent a major innovation and markedly expand the therapeutic potential of genome editing in oncology. In this review, we summarize the mechanistic basis of CRISPR-based editing, delineate design principles and engineering strategies for stimuli-responsive delivery, and highlight recent advances, outstanding challenges, and future directions toward clinical translation. We aim to provide a concise reference to guide the rational design of gene-editing cancer therapeutics.

item.title: The road ahead for stem cell therapies in type 1 diabetes.
item.abstract:
AIMS: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells. Although exogenous insulin remains the standard treatment, it does not restore physiological glucose regulation. Differentiation of human pluripotent stem cells into β-cells offers a scalable alternative to cadaveric islet transplantation and has progressed rapidly over the past decade, resulting in nine clinical trials at various stages of completion. Despite this progress, durable graft function remains constrained by two major challenges: the absence of key islet microenvironment components, such as vasculature, extracellular matrix and supporting cell types and continued vulnerability to autoimmune and alloimmune rejection.
METHODS & RESULTS: This review considers emerging technological approaches to overcome these barriers. Bioengineered niches, including multilineage organoids, functionalized hydrogels, decellularized matrices and bioprinting, aim to recreate the native islet microenvironment, while synthetic biology approaches, such as hypoimmune gene editing, CRISPR-based transcriptional control and stimulus-responsive survival circuits, seek to enhance grafts' resilience. Computational and single-cell approaches, including gene regulatory network analysis and digital twin frameworks, are beginning to provide predictive tools for benchmarking differentiation quality and forecasting graft outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Together, these complementary strategies, potentially tailored to individual patients, represent a realistic path towards safer, more effective and durable β-cell replacement therapies for type 1 diabetes.

item.title: Evolutionarily reinforced GC-rich motif enables non-AUG translation in mammals under eIF1/5MP-mediated fidelity control.
item.abstract: Non-AUG translation contributes to proteome diversity, but its regulatory principles remain unclear. Here, we show that a GCC-rich upstream extension, termed the NAT1 motif, acts as a potent enhancer of near-cognate initiation in mammals. Cell-free and reporter assays revealed that eIF1 and 5MP act as conserved inhibitors of non-AUG initiation across mammals and plants, while the NAT1 motif enables enhanced initiation within this fidelity framework. Mutational analysis identified -6 and -7 positions within the GCC repeat as key determinants of motif activity. Genome-wide analyses uncovered evolutionary depletion of NAT1-type non-AUG codons in human 5'UTRs, suggesting purifying selection against excessive initiation. Nevertheless, more than a hundred retained sites are associated with genes involved in cell proliferation and migration, suggesting that regulated non-AUG initiation may contribute to disease-relevant translational programs. The motif's enrichment within GCC repeats further suggests a mechanistic link to repeat-associated non-AUG translation.

item.title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material
item.abstract: Vision AI and robotics pick what’s worth recovering out of conveyor belts of used clothing, bottles and mixed recyclables, diverting thousands of tons of materials from landfills.

cards.score_reason: 视觉AI回收，弱相关
cards.title_cn: AI视觉与机器人助力回收业将混合废弃物转化为可再利用材料
cards.one_liner: NVIDIA报道称，视觉AI与机器人可从混合可回收物传送带上分拣出有价值材料，减少填埋。
key_findings: 视觉AI与机器人协同，在传送带上识别并分拣旧衣物、瓶子等混合可回收物。
该方案已实现数千吨材料免于进入填埋场。
cards.why_it_matters: 对合成生物学而言，高纯度、可追溯的回收原料是微生物发酵与酶解路线的关键上游；AI分拣可稳定废物流组分，值得关注其与生物炼制衔接的可能。
